items.why: The negation is explicit, and the competitor is the action Jeroboam does perform.
The passage identifies the man of God as the declarer, but the question’s pronouns are awkward.
The summary explicitly credits David and his men with all four defeats, unlike the single killer named.
The officer is clearly the antecedent of “him,” while the man of God only foretells his fate.
The sons saddle the donkey, but the old prophet explicitly mounts it.
The first covenant’s three parties are directly contrasted with the second covenant’s two.
Jotham’s succession is the event stated immediately after Uzziah’s burial.
The passage explicitly gives the Lord’s affliction as the reason, though the priests’ action is nearby.
The king’s quoted reconstruction clearly places entering the city after taking people alive.
Their final decision to surrender at the Aramean camp clearly rejects entering the city.
Sibbekai’s killing appears in the first of the two ordered Gob battles.
“What is later reported?” is vague, and “the news” is an underspecified answer.
Jeroboam’s command “Seize him” plainly targets the man of God.
Uzziah enters first, and Azariah with the other priests explicitly follows him.
The quoted plan directly contrasts eating one son today with the other tomorrow.
Zechariah is explicitly the one who instructs Uzziah in the fear of God.
Elisha’s direct reply to the officer is that he will see the food but not eat it.
The man explicitly grounds his refusal in the Lord’s command.
Talking until daylight is the last stated action before Paul leaves.
Mobilizing the army clearly precedes marching and laying siege.
The active subject “he” is Jehoiada, while David is only the former owner of the weapons.
The writer explicitly orders the man’s accusers to present their case.
The stated purpose is to make Uzziah king, though “take” makes the phrasing slightly unnatural.
The 307,500 men are explicitly under the command of the 2,600 family leaders.
The traveler killed by the lion is the man of God, not the prophet who saddled the donkey.
The officer assigned to the gate is explicitly trampled there and dies.
The two off-duty companies receive the temple-guarding command, though the long instructions are syntactically dense.
The letter heading unambiguously names Claudius Lysias as sender and Felix as recipient.
Abishai rescues David by explicitly striking down the Philistine Ishbi-Benob.
After acknowledging wrongdoing, the men explicitly decide to report to the palace at once.
Paul directly says the young man has something to tell the commander.
The messengers’ return and report occur immediately before the people plunder the camp.
The pronoun in “he loved the soil” clearly refers to Uzziah, though the question is somewhat indirect.
The speaker explicitly says “my son” was cooked and eaten before the other child was requested.
The king asks, but the man of God explicitly performs the intercession.
The three groups God helps Uzziah against are listed explicitly, while the Ammonites bring tribute.
The prophet first brings the body to his city and only afterward lays it in his tomb.
Joash is plainly the son hidden with his nurse for six years.
The text directly links the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, not merely to the rejoicing.
The commander calls two centurions and gives them the preparation order.
The Arameans believe the hired Hittite and Egyptian kings will attack them.
“This murderer” refers to the king who sends the messenger, though the referent is inferential.
In the old prophet’s claim, “him” is the man of God who is to return and eat.
Paul’s intention to leave the next day is explicitly given as the reason he speaks so long.
The non-cavalry soldiers return while the cavalry continues, though “soldiers” can broadly include cavalry.
The attacked plural group—the seven sons—runs away naked and bleeding.
Evil spirits explicitly leave, but “on the items’ arrival” is unnatural and illnesses also cease.
The conspirators ask the council to petition the commander, who is to bring Paul.
After gathering their scrolls, the practitioners immediately burn them publicly.
The explicit sword order targets followers, but the woman is also subsequently put to death.
Athaliah goes to the people after hearing their noise; seeing the king happens afterward.
The conspirators await consent, but Paul’s later arrival is also a necessary precursor to their attack.
The warning is addressed directly to the man of God from Judah.
The prophecy explicitly names Josiah as the one who will sacrifice the high-place priests.
